newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cambodia's exiled prince on way back to France.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's exiled prince on way back to France.

text.p: Cambodia's exiled Prince Norodom Sirivudh was due in Paris late on Thursday after abandoning a bid to fly home to contest charges that he plotted to kill Cambodian Co-Premier Hun Sen, his sister Norodom Vacheara said.
Vacheara told Reuters the prince was due to land at Roissy-Charles de Gaulle airport north of Paris at 10.50 p.m. (2050 GMT). She said he would press on with his attempts to clear his name.

Sirivudh flew to Hong Kong on Monday but airlines banned him from flying on to Phnom Penh after Cambodia said he would be arrested on arrival. He left Hong Kong for Europe on a Lufthansa flight on Thursday.
"He is very disappointed, very angry. He has the right to return home. He will continue fighting to demand that his trial be reviewed," Vacharea said.
"He only demands one thing and he had decided to go to prison while his trial was being reviewed," she said.

A half-brother of King Sihanouk and a former foreign minister, Sirivudh went into exile in France in December 1995 after being held for a month on charges of involvement in an alleged plot to kill Hun Sen.

Hun Sen, who rules in an uneasy coalition with the royalist FUNCINPEC party of Sirivudh's nephew Norodom Ranariddh, has refused to back calls for an amnesty and warned last week of violence if the prince returned. He said last December he would shoot down any plane carrying Sirivudh.
Sirivudh said in Hong Kong he did not think he would be killed when he arrived in Cambodia.
"I believe in our institutions. We have a monarchy, we have a king, we have a national assembly, we have a royal government," he said.
Fearing for passenger safety, Hong Kong's Dragonair refused to allow Sirivudh on its flight to Phnom Penh on Tuesday, and Royal Air Cambodge also barred him from flying.
"It is inadmissible that he be turned back like this, that a government could put pressure on an airline," Vacharea said.
Sirivudh, who told a French magazine recently that he could no longer afford to live in Paris, has said that Ranariddh and FUNCINPEC supported his return to Cambodia.

Vacharea said Sirivudh wanted a special commission of Cambodia's National Assembly to request that the trial be reviewed, and she could not understand why FUNCINPEC had not requested that such a commision be set up.
"Do they really want him to return? Does my brother also bother FUNCINPEC leaders? That's the big question I am asking myself," she said.
She said he would stay in Paris for a few days, then go to another undisclosed destination to keep campaigning to clear his name.

Before his return to Paris was confirmed, a source close to the case had told Reuters in Hong Kong that Sirivudh was trying to head for Beijing and had been in contact with Chinese officials to work out travel arrangements.
There had been unconfirmed rumours that he would meet Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk in Beijing.
